title: The Diary of a Nobody
author: George and Weedon Grossmith
setting: The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway, and an office in the City, across fifteen months from one April to the July of the next year; with excursions to the Mansion House, Broadstairs and Margate, a villa at Muswell Hill, a dinner at Peckham and Lupin's rooms in Bayswater
lengthNote: Twenty-four chapters — numbered I to XXIII, with the twenty-fourth headed Chapter the Last — each opened by a comic argument and made of dated entries; chapter IX covers a single evening
openingLine: Why should I not publish my diary?
summary: Charles Pooter, a City clerk of twenty-one years' standing, moves into a rented house in Holloway and begins to write down what happens to him. Almost nothing does. A boot-scraper trips his visitors, he paints the bath red and thinks he is bleeding to death, he makes a pun about Gowing coming and Cummings going and nobody laughs. His son Lupin loses one post, gains another, loses a fiancée, gains a fortune and despises his father throughout. Pooter records all of it in the same careful, aggrieved, pleased-with-himself voice, and the joke is that he keeps the score of a game he does not know he is losing. At the end his employer buys him the freehold of the house, and the last word in the book is Lupin's.
referenceStyle: chapter and diary entry: the book's own chapter numerals I to XXIII, and Chapter the Last, followed by the date printed at the head of the entry

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Diary of a Nobody (eBook 1026)
sourceText.note: A transcription of an Arrowsmith book printing described on its title page as a new edition, with Mr. Pooter's introduction and the chapter arguments. Its spellings and punctuation are kept, including to-day, to-morrow, Shakspeare, blanc-mange and misletoe. Pooter's very frequent italics are marked in the transcription with underscores, which are left out of the quotations here.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: George Grossmith wrote the diary while still playing the leading comic parts for Gilbert and Sullivan; his younger brother Weedon, a trained painter turned actor, drew the pictures and is credited as co-author.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Twenty-six instalments in Punch between May 1888 and May 1889, then an expanded volume from J. W. Arrowsmith of Bristol with twenty-six drawings by Weedon Grossmith. The book adds roughly four further months of entries.

atAGlance.label: The diarist
atAGlance.note: Twenty-one years with the firm of Perkupp, a rented six-roomed house in Holloway with the railway at the end of the garden, and two old friends who call nearly every evening without being asked.

atAGlance.label: The span
atAGlance.value: 3 April to 11 July of the following year
atAGlance.note: Fifteen months, but not continuous. The jump from 29 August to 30 October is five or six weeks of the diary torn out by somebody in the house to light a fire, and Pooter never finds out who.

structure.label: Chapters I–IV
structure.title: The scraper, the enamel paint and the Mansion House
structure.summary: Pooter takes The Laurels, resolves to keep a diary, and begins the record with tradesmen, a broken bell and a boot-scraper that throws every caller down the side steps. He falls out with Gowing and Cummings over a walk to a public-house, makes two jokes nobody wants, paints most of the house red and is astonished by an invitation to the Lord Mayor's reception, at which he falls over in front of the room.

scenes.title: We settle down in our new home
scenes.summary: The six-roomed residence, two pounds off the rent for the railway, the butterman who doubts that a City clerk can be a gentleman, and the curate's torn trousers.

scenes.title: Tradesmen and the scraper still troublesome
scenes.summary: Pitt tells him to keep his hair on, Farmerson bores through the gas-pipe, the dry rot joke convulses him for a whole night, and Stillbrook gets into the Cow and Hedge while Pooter waits outside.

scenes.title: A miserable evening at the Tank Theatre
scenes.summary: Merton's free passes turn out to be worthless, the tie falls into the pit, the enamel paint reaches the bath, and the pun on his friends' names empties the room.

scenes.title: The ball at the Mansion House
scenes.summary: A week of preparation, a fall on the back-door flags, and an evening in which Perkupp turns out to have arranged the invitation and Farmerson turns out to know a sheriff.

structure.label: Chapters V–VII
structure.title: A quarrel, a seaside holiday and a son out of work
structure.summary: Carrie states the case against her husband's conduct at the ball in one unbroken speech, the local paper prints his name as Pewter, and Gowing's stick has been enamelled black without permission. The Pooters take their holiday at Broadstairs with Lupin, who has been dismissed from the bank at Oldham. Back at home the diary itself is torn up for firewood, and Lupin announces an engagement.

scenes.title: After the Mansion House Ball
scenes.summary: The headache, the lobster, Carrie's indictment, the blackened stick, two failed corrections in the Blackfriars Bi-weekly News, and the joke about frayed shirts that the office enjoys and the shirtmaker does not.

scenes.title: The unexpected arrival home of our son
scenes.summary: Willie has become Lupin, has resigned from the bank, and has in fact been dismissed; the family holiday follows, with billiards, music halls and a game called Cutlets.

scenes.title: Some one tampers with my diary
scenes.summary: Mrs. James redecorates Carrie's taste, the neighbours throw a cracker at Pooter's hat, five or six weeks of the diary are burnt, and Perkupp finds Lupin a place.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–XIII
structure.title: Daisy Mutlar, the Irving imitations and an insulting card
structure.summary: Lupin's engagement fills the house. The Pooters give the grandest party of their lives, at which the champagne runs out just as Perkupp arrives. The engagement breaks off and is repaired, Burwin-Fosselton brings his Henry Irving make-up night after night, Padge takes the best chair and says nothing else, and Christmas brings a card that Pooter is certain was meant to insult him.

scenes.title: Daisy Mutlar sole topic of conversation
scenes.summary: A fiancée older than Lupin, a brother who does imitations for an hour without stopping, a firework evening that goes wrong, and a row between servant and charwoman over the missing pages.

scenes.title: Our first important party
scenes.summary: One evening, one chapter. Gowing greets the host by criticising his trousers, the Blondin Donkey is performed, and Mr. Perkupp arrives to find nothing left on the table.

scenes.title: Lupin falls out with Daisy Mutlar
scenes.summary: The morning after, a pun about side dishes, a blanc-mange that returns to the table at every meal for five days, and Lupin forbidding her name to be mentioned.

scenes.title: A dose of Irving imitations
scenes.summary: Burwin-Fosselton insists on the double name and the make-up, Padge laughs at other people's injuries, the odd sock joke lands with everyone but Pooter, and a long impertinent letter arrives which Lupin has already read and approved.

scenes.title: A serious discussion concerning the use and value of my diary
scenes.summary: Carrie walks out during a reading from it, the household laughs at the idea of publication, Pooter invokes Evelyn and Pepys, and the engagement is quietly on again.

scenes.title: I receive an insulting Christmas card
scenes.summary: Ten shillings offered for the sender's name, a good Christmas at his mother-in-law's, a punch in the dark, and the discovery that the card was addressed to L. Pooter all along.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVIII
structure.title: A hundred a year, a collapse of chlorates and a ball at East Acton
structure.summary: Perkupp promotes Pooter to senior clerk and raises his salary by a hundred pounds, and Lupin answers the announcement with a speech that copies its wording and doubles its figure. The Parachikka Chlorates collapse, Daisy marries Murray Posh, and Lupin is taken into Perkupp's office. A stylographic pen, a Volunteer ball and a cabman follow.

scenes.title: An unexpected promotion at the office
scenes.summary: Four days of suspense outside Perkupp's door, a hundred pounds a year, Lupin's two hundred in one day, a pony-trap, and an invitation from Gowing to a house where Gowing is not at home.

scenes.title: Lupin introduces us to Mr. Murray Posh
scenes.summary: Gowing's letter that went astray, a Sunday drive in which Lupin chaffs a cartload of roughs while his father rides backwards, and the first sight of the three-shilling hat millionaire.

scenes.title: We lose money over Lupin's advice
scenes.summary: Twenty pounds sold for two, Cummings left with the whole loss, Job Cleanands absconded, and a letter announcing Daisy's marriage to Murray Posh.

scenes.title: The dream of my life realised
scenes.summary: Lupin smashes a hat marked Posh's Patent, is taken into the firm, and Pooter lies awake planning the nails they will hammer in together.

scenes.title: We go to a Volunteer Ball
scenes.summary: The pen that oozes, an evening of civility that ends in a bill for three pounds and sixpence, and a cabman who pulls the diarist's beard while a policeman watches.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXIII and Chapter the Last
structure.title: Huttle, the séances and the freehold
structure.summary: An old schoolfellow's uncle shows Pooter his family portraits, two of which turn out to be of the dead. At Franching's dinner the American Hardfur Huttle defines respectability as insipidness and asks Pooter to agree. Lupin is dismissed for handing the firm's best client to a rival, is rewarded by the rival, and moves to Bayswater; Mrs. James brings table-turning into the house; and Perkupp closes the book by buying the Pooters their home.

scenes.title: A few awkward mistakes on my part
scenes.summary: Watney Lodge, a collie that licks the blacking off his boots, two portraits of the dead admired in the wrong terms, and a dream that everyone present refuses to hear.

scenes.title: Dinner at Franching's to meet Mr. Hardfur Huttle
scenes.summary: The ladies decline to leave the table, respectability is defined and demolished, Pooter checks his made-up tie in the glass, and Carrie says on the way home that Huttle is exactly like Lupin.

scenes.title: Lupin is discharged
scenes.summary: Crowbillon takes his custom elsewhere on Lupin's advice, Pooter writes sixteen pages to win him back, and Gylterson's engage Lupin at two hundred a year.

scenes.title: Mrs. James introduces spiritual séances
scenes.summary: A kicked shin at Sutton, a table that spells NIPUL and POSH, and a sealed question whose answer, when the seal is broken, turns out to be a joke about Pooter's age.

scenes.title: Lupin leaves us
scenes.summary: Rooms at two guineas a week, a dinner at which everyone but the Pooters knew it was full dress, and one sentence of political doubt on the drive home.

scenes.title: One of the happiest days of my life
scenes.summary: Perkupp buys the freehold of The Laurels and presents it to him, telegrams go out to Gowing and Cummings, and the post brings Lupin's news of another engagement.

characters.name: Charles Pooter
characters.role: The diarist; a senior clerk in the City and the tenant of The Laurels
characters.summary: He writes the book and is its target, without ever suspecting that the two facts are connected. He is punctual, honest, thrifty, fond of his wife, proud of his beard, and convinced that a joke is a thing you announce before you make. Every humiliation in the diary is one he wrote down himself, in his own hand, usually the same evening, because he thought it would interest posterity. That is the whole machine of the comedy: he is the prosecution's only witness and does not know he is testifying.
characters.clue: He records that he has not often made jokes, then makes one, then records how long he laughed at it.

characters.name: Caroline Pooter
characters.role: His wife; called Carrie throughout, and Caroline when he is being solemn
characters.summary: She laughs at his jokes more often than anyone else does, which is why he keeps making them. She is also the only person in the book who can beat him in an argument, and she does it once, at length, after the Mansion House ball, listing his evening's conduct item by item while he writes it all down. Her weakness is Mrs. James of Sutton, whose advice reaches the house as smocking, manicure, toy beetles on the mantelpiece and finally table-turning. Pooter's love for her is the one feeling in the diary that survives being written down.
characters.clue: She walks out of the room in the middle of a reading from the diary, and then explains that she was thinking about the laundress.

relationships.label: wife of, and his best audience
mother of, and usually on his side

characters.name: Willie Lupin Pooter
characters.role: Their son, twenty at the start of the diary, who has dropped his first name
characters.summary: He arrives home dismissed from a bank, calls his father Guv., despises Perkupp, makes two hundred pounds in a day and loses his father eighteen, gets engaged to a woman eight years older and is thrown over for a hat manufacturer, hands his father's firm's best client to a rival and is paid a commission for it. He is quick, rude, generous and entirely modern. The diary treats him as a worry; the reader can see that he is also the only person in the book who is going anywhere.
characters.clue: He kicks a new tall hat to pieces in the hall, and the lining is stamped with the name of the man who married his fiancée.

characters.name: Mr. Gowing
characters.role: An old friend who calls most evenings and never knocks
characters.summary: He complains about the smell of the paint, borrows the umbrella, walks into the room wearing two hats and Carrie's fur tippet, invites the Pooters to a party and then leaves town, and punches his host in the dark without recognising the head. He is the reason the book is not a cosy one: he is genuinely unkind, and Pooter genuinely cannot do without him. His friend Padge, who takes the best armchair and says nothing all evening except that it is right, is his contribution to the household.
characters.clue: Told that he has hurt someone, he explains that he thought he had hit a brick wall.

characters.name: Mr. Cummings
characters.role: An old friend who lives opposite, and an enthusiastic tricyclist
characters.summary: He is the gentler of the two friends and the one more easily wounded. He is ill twice without anybody calling, and both times produces the copy of the Bicycle News in which the accident was reported, as though the paper were proof that he had been slighted. He takes Gowing's fifteen pounds of Parachikka Chlorates off his hands and loses the lot. His running complaint, that illness shows you who your true friends are, is the only sustained reproach anybody in the book makes to the Pooters.
characters.clue: He explains his injuries twice by holding out the same cycling paper, and nobody has read it either time.

relationships.label: neighbour and reproachful friend of

characters.name: Mr. Perkupp
characters.role: The principal of Pooter's firm in the City
characters.summary: He is grave, courteous and slightly absurd, and Pooter's feeling for him is the nearest thing in the book to worship. He gives in Pooter's name for the Mansion House without saying so, arrives at the party at the exact moment of the Blondin Donkey, takes Lupin on out of respect for the father and dismisses him for the same reason, and at the end buys the freehold of the house. Whether this makes the ending a reward or a tip is a question the diary does not think to ask.
characters.clue: He looks into a room full of guests dressed as a pantomime donkey and says that it seems amusing.

characters.name: Sarah
characters.summary: She answers the side door, fetches the whisky, is suspected of burning the diary and accuses the charwoman of it, and tells her master to his face that he is always complaining. She has no separate story in the book, and that is worth noticing: the household whose respectability the diary defends rests on one young woman who is paid to run up and down ten steps, and whose opinion of the red enamel paint is the only honest review it gets.
characters.clue: Sent out for whisky, she brings back a bottle in newspaper and repeats the grocer's prices in front of the guest.

characters.name: Mr. Farmerson
characters.role: The Holloway ironmonger, who moves the scraper and repairs the bells
characters.summary: He is hired in chapter I because the landlord seems not worth troubling, bores through the gas-pipe, and is still owed a visit to repaint the bath when Pooter meets him at the Lord Mayor's reception with a sheriff's arm round him. His four words of reply to being snubbed — that if the one, why not the other — knock out the whole basis of Pooter's evening. He then takes a lift home in the cab and does not offer a farthing towards it.
characters.clue: At the Mansion House he introduces the diarist to a sheriff without the word Mister.

relationships.label: tradesman to, and then his better-placed equal

characters.name: Daisy Mutlar
characters.role: Lupin's fiancée, and afterwards Mrs. Murray Posh
characters.summary: She is introduced as the nicest, prettiest and most accomplished girl Lupin ever met, and Pooter's heart sinks the moment he sees her: a big young woman, he thinks at least eight years older than his son, and not even good-looking. She sings out of tune, rolls bread into pellets at supper and throws them, and within four months marries a hat manufacturer with ten thousand pounds settled on her. The book never shows her thinking; she is the shape of Lupin's ambition rather than a person he loves.
characters.clue: She is engaged, disengaged, engaged again and married to somebody else, and says almost nothing in the diary throughout.

characters.name: Murray Posh
characters.role: Of Posh's three-shilling hats; Lupin's rival, and later his patron
characters.summary: A tall, fat, nervous young man who will not ride in a hansom, he takes no active part in the business that has made him rich and gives a long and interesting account of the difficulties of manufacturing cheap hats. He marries Daisy, loses six hundred pounds on Lupin's tip, settles ten thousand each on his wife and his sister, and is finally engaged to be Lupin's brother-in-law. He is the book's picture of the money that was actually being made while Pooter was earning his hundred-pound rise.
characters.clue: The hat Lupin smashes in the hall, and the hat Lupin is wearing a fortnight later, both come from him.

characters.name: Mr. Burwin-Fosselton
characters.role: Of the Holloway Comedians; an amateur actor who resembles Henry Irving
characters.summary: He cracks the Pooters' round table by leaning on it, insists on the double name every time he is addressed, kicks Carrie's shins under it, digs a piece out of Gowing's neck in the middle of an imitation, and writes a two-page letter telling his host to acknowledge defeat and take his whipping gracefully. Pooter hands the letter to Lupin as proof of the man's character, and Lupin replies that he read it before it was sent and thinks an apology is owed.
characters.clue: He announces that he will bring the other make-up to-morrow night, and does.

characters.name: Mr. Hardfur Huttle
characters.role: An American writer, the guest of honour at Franching's dinner
characters.summary: He talks for an entire chapter, keeps the ladies at the table, and states the case against the Pooters of the world so plainly that the room has no answer: the middle way is a vulgar half-measure, and the man who takes it will never build anything. He then describes a soft man with a soft beard and a made-up tie, and Pooter, who is wearing one, twice checks the glass. Carrie's verdict on the way home is that he is exactly like Lupin, which is the nearest the book comes to naming its own subject.
characters.clue: Asked by name to agree that respectability means dullness, the diarist bows and says he is not competent to offer an opinion.

themes.name: The portrait he does not know he is painting
themes.summary: Pooter never lies. He reports what was said and done, including the things said to him, and then adds his own view of it, and the two do not fit. He writes out an insult word for word and calls it a compliment; he copies a sentence into the diary because he thinks it perfect, and admits three lines later that it was an apology for having been insulted. The comedy needs him to be scrupulous. A dishonest diarist would simply leave the defeats out.
themes.development: The curate's torn trousers taken as a compliment in chapter I; the forgiveness letter in II; the joke about Gowing and Cummings in III; the Mansion House in IV; the odd sock in XI; the bill for civility in XVIII; and a chapter of Hardfur Huttle describing him to his face in XX.

themes.name: Respectability, and what it costs to keep up
themes.summary: Everything Pooter does is aimed at a standard he cannot quite reach and cannot afford: a front door kept locked and used only on special occasions, lavender gloves, two white ties in case one is spoiled, visiting cards ordered twenty-five at a time. The joke is not that he is a snob but that the standard itself is a trap, since every attempt to meet it produces the accident that ruins it. Huttle names the cost in one sentence, and Pooter cannot argue.
themes.development: The front door that will not open in chapter I; the dress-coat the tailor takes back for want of a shilling in IV; the paragraph about Charles Pewter in V; the party in IX; the three-pound supper bill in XVIII; and the definition of the happy medium in XX.

themes.name: Clerks, tradesmen and the people above
themes.summary: The diary is exact about money — two pounds off the rent, seven-and-six for a stick, thirty-eight shillings for a dozen of whisky, a hundred a year — and exact about rank, which is why the two keep colliding. A drunk butterman doubts that a City clerk can be a gentleman. The ironmonger who botched the scraper turns out to be on back-slapping terms with a sheriff. Pooter looks down on tradesmen and errand-boys and is looked down on by his son, his son's friends and the stockbroking world that is making the real money.
themes.development: Borset in chapter I; Merton on Society in III; Farmerson at the Mansion House in IV; Posh's three-shilling hats in XV; the six-hundred-pound loss in XVI; Lupin's two hundred a year in XXI; and one radical thought in the carriage in XXIII.

themes.name: The Laurels, and the work of keeping it up
themes.summary: The house is the book's real subject: six rooms and a basement, rented, with the railway at the bottom of the garden and a wall already cracking. Pooter hammers, paints, plants mustard-and-cress, repairs the cornice and alters the stair-carpets, and half the comedy comes from the house resisting. He is happiest doing this and says so plainly. The ending hands him the freehold, which is either the reward the diary has earned or the proof that his life was always in another man's gift.
themes.development: The tin-tack and the Venetian blind in chapter I; the enamel paint in III; the chimney-glass bought with the rise in XIV; the cistern and the cornice in XVIII and XXII; Lupin's opinion that Brickfield Terrace is a bit off in XXIII; and Perkupp's gift in Chapter the Last.

themes.name: Twenty-one years at Perkupp's
themes.summary: Pooter's standing at the office is his whole claim on the world, and he states its terms twice: twenty-one years of industry and strict attention to the interests of his superiors. The book sets that against Lupin, who arrives late, takes no interest and is paid better for it, and against a market in which a tip on chlorates can make two hundred pounds in a day. Nothing in the diary argues that Pooter is wrong to have worked as he has. It simply keeps the two accounts side by side.
themes.development: Pitt's insolence in chapter II; the hundred-pound rise and Lupin's parody of the announcement in XIV; the collapse of the chlorates in XVI; the sixteen-page letter to Crowbillon in XXI; and Gylterson's offer of two hundred a year to a young man who has been at it a few weeks.

themes.name: The war with things
themes.summary: Objects in Holloway are hostile and very nearly animate. A boot-scraper trips four separate callers and is finally moved by a man who bores through the gas-pipe. A bell rings in the wrong room, then has no handle, then does not exist when it is needed. Enamel paint dissolves in a hot bath. A stylographic pen oozes ink and gets somebody else blamed. The pattern lets Pooter keep his dignity by blaming the equipment, and it is also an exact account of a household run on a small budget.
themes.development: The scraper and the bells through chapters I and II; the red enamel through III; Gowing's stick in V; the antimacassar in VII; the blanc-mange in X; the stylographic pen and the cistern in XVIII.

themes.name: Friendship as a standing arrangement
themes.summary: Gowing and Cummings come in without knocking, eat the supper, mock the host, and are the fixed points of his week. Nobody in the book says a word about affection. What holds the three together is habit and the side entrance, and the diary keeps score — who called, who did not, who was ill and not visited, whose stick was ruined. It is a truthful picture of male friendship kept up for twenty years on very little, and the book is generous enough to make it look worth having.
themes.development: The walk to the Cow and Hedge in chapter II; the letters of forgiveness in II; the blackened stick in V; the party at which they eat as though starved in IX; Cummings's reproaches in XIV and XVIII; and the telegrams sent on the last day.

techniques.name: The diary form
techniques.definition: A narrative built from dated entries written close to the events, so that the teller has no hindsight, no chance to shape the story and no way of leaving anything out that he has not yet learnt to be ashamed of.
techniques.inThisBook: Everything depends on it. Pooter writes up the evening's humiliation the same night, while it still feels like a triumph, and the entry is what convicts him. The form also supplies the running gags free of charge, since a scraper or a blanc-mange can simply reappear on the next date, and it produces one perfect accident: he notices the following morning that he wrote retired tired, thinks it rather funny, and says that if he were not so worried he might have made a joke of it.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: A gap between what the speaker understands and what the audience can see, held open long enough for the audience to do the judging.
techniques.inThisBook: The gap is never closed by a second narrator, because there is not one. The reader assembles the other view from the evidence Pooter files: the silence after his best joke, the guests' laughter at something they will not explain, Perkupp's remark that the foolery seems amusing. The Grossmiths take the risk that the reader will see nothing, and rely entirely on our knowing what a room looks like when it has stopped finding you funny.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A drop from the elevated to the trivial, usually at the end of a sentence or a passage.
techniques.inThisBook: The diarist builds the flight himself and then falls out of it. He is bleeding to death like Marat in the waxworks until he remembers the enamel paint. He is a proud man leading his pretty wife to the Lord Mayor until his boots go from under him. His sixteen closely written pages come back as sixteen lines. The pattern is so regular that by the middle of the book the reader starts bracing for the last clause of every entry.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.definition: Puns, near-homophones and turns on a word, made for their own sake and judged by the response they get.
techniques.inThisBook: Pooter's puns are the book's cruellest device, because they are funny twice over: once as puns and once as evidence. He gets into a scrape about a scraper, tells Gowing he is talking dry rot, finds that Gowing is always coming and Cummings always going, and is amazed when the room goes quiet. He records the laughter carefully, and the record shows that the only reliable laugher is his wife.

techniques.name: Comic repetition
techniques.definition: A detail brought back at intervals until the return itself, rather than the detail, is what raises the laugh.
techniques.inThisBook: The scraper claims Cummings, Gowing, the curate and the butcher in the first two chapters. The blanc-mange comes back to the table for five days, disguised at last in a glass dish with jam round it. Padge says that it is right, and nothing else, for two whole evenings. Cummings produces the same cycling paper twice, years apart in feeling if not in time. The diary form makes all of this effortless: a date is enough to bring the thing back.

techniques.name: The unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator whose account the reader learns to read against, because he misjudges himself or the meaning of what he reports.
techniques.inThisBook: Pooter is accurate about facts and wrong about their weight. He quotes insults verbatim and files them under friendship, calls a snub a compliment, and reports his own jokes alongside the exact length of the silence that followed. Nothing is hidden and nothing is admitted, so the reader is left holding two versions of every evening — which is also, in practice, what it is like to read anybody's diary.

techniques.name: Pooter's prose
techniques.definition: A style so particular to one speaker that a sentence can be identified without the name attached.
techniques.inThisBook: The voice is made of a few habits: the apologetic by-the-by, the offered reward (ten shillings, half-a-sovereign) for information nobody will give, the phrase I am a poor man used before spending, the solemn adverbs (I simply said, I replied coolly, I treated the observation with silence), and italics laid on so thickly that the emphasis stops meaning anything. It is a clerk's prose — careful, hedged, slightly legal — applied to a boot-scraper.

quotations.text: Why should I not publish my diary? I have often seen reminiscences of people I have never even heard of, and I fail to see—because I do not happen to be a ‘Somebody’—why my diary should not be interesting.
quotations.speaker: Charles Pooter
quotations.context: The whole of Pooter's preface, signed and dated from The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway, before the diary proper begins.
quotations.analysis: The book's title is answered before the book starts, and the answer is a question nobody asked. Pooter argues from a real grievance — celebrated nobodies publish their memories, so why not an uncelebrated one — and the argument is perfectly sound; it is the tone that gives him away, the defensive dash, the sniff at ‘Somebody’ in inverted commas. He is the first of the two brothers' jokes and the last: the reader is about to agree with him, for two hundred pages, for reasons he would not accept.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text, Introduction by Mr. Pooter

quotations.text: I restrained my feelings, and quietly remarked that I thought it was possible for a city clerk to be a gentleman. He replied he was very glad to hear it, and wanted to know whether I had ever come across one, for he hadn’t.
quotations.context: Borset the butterman, drunk in the downstairs hall, has said he will be hanged if he serves City clerks any more.
quotations.analysis: This is the book's subject stated in the first chapter by a man delivering butter. Pooter's sentence is a small masterpiece of self-defence: restrained, quietly, remarked, thought it was possible — four hedges in one line, so that the claim is barely made before it is knocked down. The riposte works because it accepts his terms and simply denies the evidence. Two sentences later he hears Borset fall over the scraper and is glad he never had it moved, and the entry ends with him thinking of a splendid answer he ought to have given, which he keeps for another occasion and never uses.

quotations.text: I don’t often make jokes, but I replied: “You’re talking a lot of dry rot yourself.” I could not help roaring at this, and Carrie said her sides quite ached with laughter. I never was so immensely tickled by anything I have ever said before. I actually woke up twice during the night, and laughed till the bed shook.
quotations.context: Gowing, who has complained about the smell of paint on every visit, announces that this time he distinctly smells dry rot.
quotations.analysis: The joke is thin and the reporting of it is enormous, and the disproportion is the comedy. Note the preface — I don't often make jokes — which he has already used once, eight days earlier, over the scraper and the scrape; it is not modesty but a flourish, a man rolling up his sleeves. Then four sentences of aftermath: roaring, aching sides, a superlative, and finally a night of it. The bed shaking in the dark is the detail that turns a weak pun into something close to tenderness, and it is also the exact measure of how little else there is to laugh at in Brickfield Terrace.

quotations.text: I thought I was the aggrieved party; but as I freely forgive you, you—feeling yourself aggrieved—should bestow forgiveness on me. … I have copied this verbatim in the diary, because I think it is one of the most perfect and thoughtful sentences I have ever written. I posted the letter, but in my own heart I felt I was actually apologising for having been insulted.
quotations.context: Cummings and Gowing left Pooter outside a public-house for the best part of an hour, and have written demanding an explanation of his conduct.
quotations.analysis: Three movements in one entry, and each undoes the one before. The sentence itself is a knot: a forgiveness that requires forgiving back, so that the injured party ends by asking pardon. Then comes the vanity, and the reason the reader gets to see the knot at all — he has copied it out because he is proud of it. Then the last line, which is the sharpest thing in the first half of the book, because it shows he knows. The diary form does all the work here. No other shape would let a man record his own cleverness and his own defeat in the same paragraph, in that order.

quotations.text: It’s concerning you both; for doesn’t it seem odd that Gowing’s always coming and Cummings’ always going? … I think this was one of the best jokes I have ever made.
quotations.speaker: Charles Pooter
quotations.context: Both friends have called on the evening of the red bath; Cummings has already said Funny as usual, without warmth.
quotations.analysis: The best-known joke in the book, and the laugh and the silence come in successive paragraphs. Carrie goes into fits and Pooter doubles up until the chair cracks; then the two men look at him without smiling, and Gowing calls a pun on a name wanting in taste. What makes it funny rather than painful is that Pooter never revises the verdict. The sentence stands in the diary unaltered.

quotations.text: My first thought was that I had ruptured an artery, and was bleeding to death, and should be discovered, later on, looking like a second Marat, as I remember seeing him in Madame Tussaud’s. My second thought was to ring the bell, but remembered there was no bell to ring. My third was, that there was nothing but the enamel paint, which had dissolved with boiling water.
quotations.context: Two days after painting the bath red, Pooter decides to treat a chill with a bath as hot as he can bear.
quotations.analysis: The structure is a countdown from tragedy to ironmongery, and the numbering does it: first, second, third, each thought smaller than the last. The middle step is the one to watch — the bell that has been broken since the first page, so that even the melodrama cannot be rung for. Marat is exactly the right reference for him, since he has not read about the murder but seen the waxwork, which is how the whole of Pooter's culture reaches him. Then the paragraph ends with the paint, and the business of the morning: he will tell Farmerson to come and paint the bath white.

quotations.text: I simply looked at him, and said coolly: “I never expected to see you here.” He said, with a loud, coarse laugh: “I like that—if you, why not me?” … Farmerson seized me rather roughly by the collar, and addressing the sheriff, said: “Let me introduce my neighbour, Pooter.” He did not even say “Mister.”
quotations.context: The supper-room at the Mansion House, where Pooter has just been slapped on the shoulder by the ironmonger who was to have repainted his bath.
quotations.analysis: Farmerson demolishes the evening in six words, and does it without malice, which is worse. Pooter's snub has assumed a ladder that the ironmonger simply does not believe in; and within five minutes a sheriff in full court costume has his arm round Farmerson's neck, so the ladder turns out not to exist. The last stroke is the smallest: the missing Mister. Pooter has spent four chapters and a great deal of money to be in that room, and he is introduced there as a neighbour by the man who mended his scraper, on first-name terms with people he cannot reach.

quotations.text: After professing to snub Mr. Farmerson, you permit him to snub you, in my presence, and then accept his invitation to take a glass of champagne with you, and you don’t limit yourself to one glass. You then offer this vulgar man, who made a bungle of repairing our scraper, a seat in our cab on the way home.
quotations.speaker: Caroline Pooter
quotations.context: The morning after the ball. Pooter has opened by asking, perfectly calmly and quietly, for a little explanation of his wife's conduct.
quotations.analysis: This is the only sustained attack on Pooter delivered by somebody who loves him, and it is the only one he transcribes in full. Carrie's method is a list in chronological order with no adjectives except vulgar, which is the word he would have used himself, and the sting is that every item is true and the reader has already seen it happen. The entry then does the thing that makes the book more than a set of jokes: he writes down the whole speech, calls himself humiliated, and does not answer it. Gowing comes in wearing two hats and calls it a lovers' quarrel.

quotations.text: “We have received two letters from Mr. and Mrs. Charles Pewter, requesting us to announce the important fact that they were at the Mansion House Ball.” I tore up the paper and threw it in the waste-paper basket. My time is far too valuable to bother about such trifles.
quotations.context: The third attempt to get his name into the Blackfriars Bi-weekly News list of guests; the second attempt printed him as Porter, so he wrote it out in capitals.
quotations.analysis: The paper has worked out what he is doing and printed it as news, with the phrase the important fact carrying the whole of the editor's opinion. The comedy then doubles back on him twice. He has written twice and ordered a dozen copies to send to friends, so the sneer is exactly earned; and his closing line about his time being too valuable arrives after three entries spent on nothing else. The misspellings are the crudest of jokes — Porter, Pewter — and the best, because a man whose name cannot survive a typesetter has no business worrying about the Lord Mayor.

quotations.text: Imagine my dismay when he replied with a loud guffaw: “It’s no use. If you want the good old truth, I’ve got the chuck!”
quotations.speaker: Lupin Pooter
quotations.context: Lupin has just announced that he has tendered his resignation at the bank, and his father has ordered him to sit down and withdraw it at dictation.
quotations.analysis: Two Englishes collide in one exchange. The father's is formal and futile — how dare you, sir; you will sit down immediately; amply apologising for your thoughtlessness — the language of a man who believes an employer can be written to. The son's is four syllables of slang that cancel the whole speech. The guffaw matters: Lupin is not ashamed, and the reader can see what Pooter cannot, that the resignation was a face-saving lie which his father's pomposity has just forced him to drop. Five days later Pooter records that being sacked for idleness is, on the whole, satisfactory.

quotations.text: I was a little vexed at everybody subsequently laughing at some joke which they did not explain, and it was only on going to bed I discovered I must have been walking about all the evening with an antimacassar on one button of my coat-tails.
quotations.context: An evening of card games with Mrs. James and Gowing, during which Lupin has led Gowing to a looking-glass and called the game monkeys.
quotations.analysis: The perfect emblem of the book, and Pooter files it without comment. The sentence is built to delay: a little vexed, a joke not explained, and then the discovery at bedtime, hours too late to do anything but write it down. An antimacassar is the most domestic object in the house, the cloth that protects a chair-back from hair-oil, and he has been dragging respectability's own furnishing round the room behind him. He works it out in the end, which is the part readers tend to forget. He simply works it out too late, every time, and keeps the record anyway.

quotations.text: I should very much like to know who has wilfully torn the last five or six weeks out of my diary. It is perfectly monstrous! Mine is a large scribbling diary, with plenty of space for the record of my everyday events, and in keeping up that record I take (with much pride) a great deal of pains.
quotations.context: The entry that follows a jump of two months. A burnt scrap in the grate turns out to be part of the diary.
quotations.analysis: The book eats itself, and the reader feels the hole before the explanation arrives, since the last entry was in August. Pooter's defence of the diary is his defence of himself — large, plenty of space, much pride, a great deal of pains — and the household's verdict is delivered by the fire: it was the handiest paper for lighting one. He never discovers who did it, and the inquiry runs through the servant, the charwoman and the sweep, all of whom deny it and none of whom is believed. The following day he admits that the missing weeks held nothing but rejection letters for Lupin.

quotations.text: I apologised for the foolery, but Mr. Perkupp said: “Oh, it seems amusing.” I could see he was not a bit amused.
quotations.context: The Pooters' first important party. Lupin and Frank Mutlar have just burst in as the Blondin Donkey, one of them whitened like a clown.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three levels of knowledge, and for once Pooter is on the reader's level. He sees the politeness for what it is, which is why the entry is not comic relief but the hinge of the chapter: the hour he has planned for since the invitations went out arrives while there is a pantomime donkey in the drawing-room. The economy is worth noticing — the joke needs no adjective, only the flat repetition of amusing and amused, with a negative dropped into it. Downstairs the table is a wreck, and the great man asks for soda water and is offered port.

quotations.text: When I returned to the parlour, Gowing was retailing his idiotic joke about the odd sock, and Carrie was roaring with laughter. I suppose I am losing my sense of humour.
quotations.context: The laundress has sent back an odd sock, and Gowing has suggested giving it to a poor man with one leg.
quotations.analysis: The saddest line in the book, and it is a joke. Gowing's remark is no better than anything Pooter has produced — arguably worse — and the difference is entirely in the delivery and in who is making it. Pooter's conclusion is exactly the wrong one, since his sense of humour is unimpaired; what has failed is his standing. The verb retailing carries the grievance: Gowing is selling the joke round the house, and Carrie, who has laughed at dry rot until her sides ached, is buying. Then Pooter goes back to complaining about Padge, which is what a man does when he cannot say the true thing.

quotations.text: I am sure it would prove quite as interesting as some of the ridiculous reminiscences that have been published lately. Besides, it’s the diary that makes the man. Where would Evelyn and Pepys have been if it had not been for their diaries? … Lupin, in a jeering tone, said: “If it had been written on larger paper, Guv., we might get a fair price from a butterman for it.”
quotations.context: At breakfast, after Carrie has said plainly that no publisher would take it and both she and Lupin have burst out laughing.
quotations.analysis: The book turns and looks at itself. Pooter's defence is the one he made in his preface, and it is not as silly as his family thinks: the diary did make Pepys. What he cannot see is the joke inside his own sentence, because it's the diary that makes the man is true of him in a way he would hate. Lupin answers by the weight of the paper.

quotations.text: I am a poor man, but I would gladly give ten shillings to find out who sent me the insulting Christmas card I received this morning. I never insult people; why should they insult me?
quotations.context: Christmas Eve. The handwriting on the envelope slopes the wrong way, and Pooter begins to work through his acquaintance.
quotations.analysis: Two of his favourite forms in one sentence: the declaration of poverty made just before an offer of money, and the reward for information, which he has already posted once, at the same rate, for the person who tore up his diary. The second sentence is a child's logic and is perfectly sincere. The payoff comes five days later, after a dream, a comparison of handwriting and a formal accusation: Carrie points out that the card was addressed to L. Pooter, and Lupin cheerfully admits he gets such cards, and sends them. The offence was never aimed at him at all.

quotations.text: My boy, as a result of twenty-one years’ industry and strict attention to the interests of my superiors in office, I have been rewarded with promotion and a rise in salary of £100. … “Having been in the firm of Job Cleanands, stock and share-brokers, a few weeks, and not having paid particular attention to the interests of my superiors in office, my Guv’nor, as a reward to me, allotted me £5 worth of shares in a really good thing. The result is, to-day I have made £200.”
quotations.context: A bottle of Jackson Frères has been opened at supper to celebrate news that father and son each claim to have.
quotations.analysis: The best-built joke in the book, and it belongs to Lupin. He stands up, takes his father's exact syntax and swaps in his own facts: twenty-one years becomes a few weeks, strict attention becomes not having paid particular attention, a hundred pounds a year becomes two hundred in a day. Nothing is said about what the parody means. The two sentences are left side by side for the reader to compare.

quotations.text: I was not so sanguine as to suppose, as you predicted, that I should get six or eight times the amount of my investment; still a profit of £2 is a good percentage for such a short time. … Lupin said, quite irritably: “You don’t understand. I sold your £20 shares for £2; you therefore lose £18 on the transaction.
quotations.context: The Parachikka Chlorates have collapsed. Lupin has just explained that he was fortunate to get two pounds for his father's holding.
quotations.analysis: A whole economy fits into a misread figure. Pooter hears the word profit and does his sum from the only kind of money he has ever handled, the kind that goes up by ten pounds a year; the possibility that an investment can return less than nothing has not occurred to him. The word irritably is beautifully placed — the son is annoyed at having to explain a loss he caused — and the sentence that follows completes the ruin by adding Cummings and Gowing, who will lose the lot. The eighteen pounds is roughly a fifth of the rise he was given six weeks earlier.

quotations.text: I made myself useful, and assisted several ladies to ices, remembering an old saying that “There is nothing lost by civility.” … “Your party’s had four suppers at 5s. a head, five ices at 1s., three bottles of champagne at 11s. 6d., a glass of claret, and a sixpenny cigar for the stout gentleman—in all £3 0s. 6d.!”
quotations.context: The East Acton Volunteer ball. Pooter has been handing round wine in an empty supper-room, assuming that a private invitation covers the food.
quotations.analysis: His one virtue is itemised and priced, and the bill is the funniest document in the book precisely because it is accurate. The proverb is doing the damage: he is not being generous, he is investing in a saying, and the waiter's list turns the investment into pounds, shillings and pence. The stout gentleman is Padge, who has said nothing all evening except that it is right, and whose cigar Pooter is now paying for. Three pounds and sixpence is a great deal of money for the household; he cannot cover it, gives his card, and resolves to keep the misfortune from Carrie so as not to spoil her evening.

quotations.text: I said to Mr. Finsworth: “Who is this jovial-looking gentleman? Life doesn’t seem to trouble him much.” Mr. Finsworth said: “No, it doesn’t. He is dead too—my brother.”
quotations.context: At Watney Lodge, Muswell Hill. Pooter has already said of a crayon portrait that the face looked pinched, and been told it was drawn after death.
quotations.analysis: The second blunder is the joke; the first only sets the trap. Having walked into one death, he crosses the room to a cheerful red face in a straw hat and volunteers the remark guaranteed to be wrong twice over. The comedy is in the host's flat too, quietly counting the bodies. This is the book at its most generous: not a fool, only a man in a strange drawing-room with nothing to say.

quotations.text: I am getting quite accustomed to being snubbed by Lupin, and I do not mind being sat upon by Carrie, because I think she has a certain amount of right to do so; but I do think it hard to be at once snubbed by wife, son, and both my guests.
quotations.context: He has tried to tell the room about a dream of burning ice, and been told by four people in turn that other people's dreams are of no interest.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a man drawing up the terms of his own defeat and finding them, on the whole, acceptable. The concession to Carrie is the heart of it — she has a certain amount of right to do so — which is both a joke about a henpecked husband and a genuine statement of how he sees his marriage. What he objects to is not the snubbing but the arithmetic: four at once is too many. The dream itself, blocks of ice on fire, is the single imaginative thing he produces in the book, and it is exactly what nobody will let him have.

quotations.text: The happy medium means respectability, and respectability means insipidness. Does it not, Mr. Pooter?” I was so taken aback by being personally appealed to, that I could only bow apologetically, and say I feared I was not competent to offer an opinion.
quotations.speaker: Mr. Hardfur Huttle, then Charles Pooter
quotations.context: Franching's dinner at Peckham. Huttle has been asked to explain the phrase happy medium, which his hostess offered as a pleasantry.
quotations.analysis: The book's case for the prosecution, delivered at a dinner table and addressed by name to the defendant. Huttle is rude, loud and largely right, and the Grossmiths give him the best rhetoric in the novel before letting him overreach: within a page he has insulted a deaf woman, the host's champagne and a man who spends his evenings playing dominoes with his wife, which is Pooter exactly. The reply is the finest thing Pooter ever says without meaning to. Bow apologetically and not competent to offer an opinion are the manners of the clerk, produced under direct attack, and they prove Huttle's point and answer it in the same breath.

quotations.text: I always feel people are happier who live a simple unsophisticated life. I believe I am happy because I am not ambitious.
quotations.context: The last lines of the chapter, written in bed after the dinner, following Carrie's remark that Huttle is exactly like Lupin.
quotations.analysis: Pooter's creed, stated plainly for once, straight after the man who despises it has finished talking. By itself the sentence is not ridiculous, and the book has been quietly showing that he is in fact happy. The placing undercuts it twice: he is ambitious, as chapter VI admits about getting his son into the firm, and he has just spent an evening trying to please a man with money.

quotations.text: I wrote him sixteen pages, closely written; he wrote me less than sixteen lines. … “Sir,—I totally disagree with you. Your son, in the course of five minutes’ conversation, displayed more intelligence than your firm has done during the last five years.
quotations.context: Perkupp has asked Pooter to write privately to Crowbillon, the firm's most valued client, and win him back. It took a whole day.
quotations.analysis: Pooter measures his own effort the only way he knows, by quantity, and the repetition of sixteen sets up the fall before the letter is even opened. Crowbillon's reply is a model of what he is up against: five lines, no courtesy, and a comparison of five minutes with five years that reverses everything the diary believes about long service. Pooter's response is not anger but a practical difficulty — he dare not show it to Perkupp and would not show it to Lupin — and he is left holding a document that proves his master wrong and his son right. He reports the contents to Perkupp in a modified form.

quotations.text: On the way home in the carriage, for the first time in my life, I was inclined to indulge in the radical thought that money was not properly divided.
quotations.context: Riding home in Murray Posh's carriage after dinner at Lupin's new rooms, having just been told what Posh has settled on his wife and his sister.
quotations.analysis: One sentence of political doubt in a book with no politics, and it is placed with great care: in a rich man's carriage, going back to a rented house in Holloway, at the end of an evening in which a necklace costing three hundred pounds has been mentioned. The hedging is the whole character — inclined to indulge in, and the word radical held at arm's length, as if the thought belonged to somebody disreputable. He does not develop it. The next paragraph is about a cab waiting outside his house, and the idea never appears again. Six days later he is given a house and the question is closed.

quotations.text: Mr. Perkupp, to my surprise, said: “Mr. Pooter, I will purchase the freehold of that house, and present it to the most honest and most worthy man it has ever been my lot to meet.”
quotations.speaker: Mr. Perkupp
quotations.context: The final entry but one. Pooter has just been thanked for the service he did the firm through Hardfur Huttle's American connection.
quotations.analysis: The ending refuses to be a punchline. Pooter has wanted two things throughout, his house and his employer's good opinion, and he is given both in one sentence, in the exact terms he would have chosen. It can be read as the comedy relenting or as the last irony, since a man's home is still a gift in another man's hands. The diary offers no verdict.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text, Chapter the Last

timeline.label: Punch begins publication
timeline.detail: The weekly that would print the diary in twenty-six instalments, read largely by the professional and clerical households it made its subject.

timeline.label: George Grossmith is born in London
timeline.detail: On 9 December, son of a police-court reporter. He worked at Bow Street himself before making a living on the platform as a comic singer at the piano.

timeline.label: Weedon Grossmith is born in London
timeline.detail: On 9 June. He trained as a painter and exhibited before turning to the stage, and is credited as co-author of the book as well as its illustrator.

timeline.label: George Grossmith joins the Gilbert and Sullivan company
timeline.detail: He created John Wellington Wells in The Sorcerer and went on to the run of leading comic parts, among them Sir Joseph Porter, Bunthorne, the Lord Chancellor and Ko-Ko.

timeline.label: The Cheap Trains Act
timeline.detail: Railway companies are obliged to run workmen's trains at low fares, one of the pressures that turned districts such as Holloway into streets of small rented villas — with, as at The Laurels, the line at the end of the garden and two pounds off the rent.

timeline.label: The 'Is Marriage a Failure?' press correspondence
timeline.detail: Set off by Mona Caird's article on marriage in the Westminster Review that August and carried on at length in the daily press. Pooter and Carrie talk it over on 2 November and agree that it has been no failure in their case.

timeline.label: The serial begins in Punch
timeline.detail: Twenty-six instalments between May 1888 and May 1889, written by George Grossmith while he was still playing nightly for D'Oyly Carte.

timeline.label: George Grossmith leaves the D'Oyly Carte company
timeline.detail: After twelve years of comic leads he returned to touring as a solo entertainer, which had been his living before Gilbert and Sullivan and remained more profitable.

timeline.label: The Eiffel Tower opens in Paris
timeline.detail: Named by Hardfur Huttle at Franching's dinner, beside the Brooklyn Bridge, as the kind of thing a man of the happy medium will never build.

timeline.label: J. W. Arrowsmith publishes the book in Bristol
timeline.detail: Expanded by roughly four months of entries and illustrated with twenty-six drawings by Weedon Grossmith. The same firm had published Three Men in a Boat three years earlier.

timeline.label: A new issue carries prefatory tributes
timeline.detail: The early book editions attracted little notice; the 1910 issue, with appreciations by Lord Rosebery and Augustine Birrell, marks the point at which the book's standing was made by admirers rather than by sales.

timeline.label: George Grossmith dies at Folkestone
timeline.detail: On 1 March. He had published two volumes of reminiscence of his own, which is one of the jokes behind Pooter's preface.

timeline.label: Weedon Grossmith dies
timeline.detail: On 14 June, after a second career as actor, playwright and theatre manager, and a memoir of his own about the move from painting to the stage.

timeline.label: Ken Russell films the diary for the BBC
timeline.detail: Made for the arts programme Monitor and played as a silent comedy with captions, which suits a book whose narrator cannot hear how he sounds.

timeline.label: A four-part adaptation on BBC Four
timeline.detail: With Hugh Bonneville as Pooter speaking the entries straight to camera, the nearest television has come to reproducing the effect of the diary form.

places.name: Holloway, north London
places.note: The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, is invented, but the district is not: streets of small rented villas built for clerks, with the Great Northern line close enough to crack the garden wall.

places.name: The Mansion House, City of London
places.note: The Lord Mayor's reception for the representatives of trades and commerce, where Pooter meets his ironmonger, drinks champagne with a sheriff and falls over in the middle of a waltz.

places.name: Broadstairs, Kent
places.note: The family's usual holiday. Apartments near the station rather than on the cliffs, because the cliffs are double the price; Lupin objects to the fly in the butter.

places.name: Margate, Kent
places.note: Where the Cummings are staying, and where Gowing's game of Cutlets ends with the whole party on the floor and Carrie's head against the fender.

places.name: Muswell Hill
places.note: Watney Lodge, the house of Mr. Edgar Paul Finsworth, a few minutes from the station: a collie, a spaniel called Bibbs, water-colours of India and two portraits of the dead.

places.name: Sutton, Surrey
places.note: Home of Mrs. James, whose visits bring smocking, manicure, toy beetles on the mantelpiece and finally table-turning into The Laurels.

places.name: Peckham
places.note: Mr. Franching's house, a long way from Holloway by two omnibuses, and the setting for the dinner at which Hardfur Huttle defines respectability.

places.name: Bayswater
places.note: Lupin's furnished apartments at two guineas a week, taken to be near the Murray Poshes and because, in his phrase, Brickfield Terrace is a bit off.

criticalViews.position: A magazine joke at the expense of the suburban clerk
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the book is Punch doing what Punch did: holding up a type — the villa, the pretensions, the unfunny jokes, the visiting cards — so that a readership slightly above him could enjoy the distance. The title says as much. Pooter is a nobody, and the comedy asks the reader to agree.
criticalViews.counter: The book will not stay in that shape. Pooter is the only person in it who works hard, keeps his word, pays his way and loves his wife, and the people who laugh at him — Gowing, Padge, Burwin-Fosselton, Job Cleanands — are worse company by every measure the book itself applies. A satire on the suburbs would not have ended by giving him the house.

criticalViews.position: The comedy exists only in the gap between his account and ours
criticalViews.summary: Every laugh is produced by the same engine: the diary reports faithfully, the narrator interprets wrongly, and the reader takes the report and discards the interpretation. On this view the form is the whole invention, and Pooter is less a character than a hole in the page through which the reader looks.
criticalViews.counter: He closes the gap more often than the reading allows. He knows he was apologising for having been insulted; he knows the sock joke was no worse than his own; he writes down one radical thought about money and puts it away. Those moments are not lapses in the machine, they are why the book can be read twice.

criticalViews.position: A record of a class on the move, and of what the movement cost
criticalViews.summary: The diary prices everything — rent, gloves, whisky, cards, a hundred-pound rise, two hundred pounds made in a day on chlorates — and read as social history it catches an exact moment: salaried respectability being overtaken by speculation, advertising and cheap manufacture, with Posh's three-shilling hats worth more than twenty-one years of service.
criticalViews.counter: Read that way the book loses its timing. The chlorates and the hats are there, but so is a man laughing in the dark at his own pun about dry rot, and the second thing is what has kept the book alive. There is also a limit to its social range: the servant Sarah and the charwoman Mrs. Birrell are inside the house and outside the sympathy, and the diary never wonders what they make of any of it.

essayQuestions.question: How do the Grossmiths make a man funny without letting him know he is being funny?
essayQuestions.focus: The diary form, dramatic irony and the reader's share of the work
plan: Set out the mechanism with the forgiveness letter in chapter II: a sentence copied out because he is proud of it, followed by the admission that it was an apology for an insult.
Show the reader doing the assembling in chapter III, where the silence after the pun on his friends' names is reported but never interpreted.
Argue that the form does what a second narrator would do elsewhere, and that the dated entry removes hindsight — he cannot tidy Tuesday on Wednesday.
Test the reading against the moments when he does see, such as the odd sock and the antimacassar, and ask whether those weaken the comedy or deepen it.
Conclude on the risk the method runs: nothing is underlined, so a reader who misses the silence misses the book.

essayQuestions.question: Are we invited to laugh at Charles Pooter, or to like him? Can the book do both?
plan: Begin with the case for satire: the title, the magazine it appeared in, and the relentless exposure of his snobbery towards tradesmen and errand-boys.
Set against it the conduct of the people who mock him — Gowing's punch in the dark, Burwin-Fosselton's letter, Lupin's parody of the promotion speech.
Analyse the marriage, and Carrie's speech after the ball, as the one relationship the diary cannot make ridiculous.
Read the gift of the freehold in Chapter the Last both ways: as the comedy relenting, and as the last and quietest joke about dependence.
Decide whether the two readings can be held together, and what it means that the book's final words belong to Lupin.

essayQuestions.question: What is the book's attitude to Lupin, and to the world he represents?
plan: Trace Lupin's fortunes: dismissed from a bank, two hundred pounds in a day, an engagement broken, a client handed to a rival and a commission paid for it.
Analyse the promotion speech in chapter XIV as a formal parody, and show what it does to the value of twenty-one years' service.
Set Hardfur Huttle beside him, and weigh Carrie's verdict that the American is a second Lupin, older and more influential.
Consider Crowbillon's five lines against Pooter's sixteen pages as the book's judgement on the contest between the two.
Ask whether the Grossmiths admire, fear or simply record the new money, and whether the collapse of the chlorates answers the question.

essayQuestions.question: How much of the comedy comes from objects, and what does that tell us about the household?
essayQuestions.focus: Things, money and the maintenance of respectability
plan: Follow the scraper through the first two chapters, counting its victims, and note how it is finally removed at the cost of a gas-pipe.
Read the red enamel paint as the book's central set piece, from flower-pots to the backs of the Shakspeare to the bath and the second Marat.
Add the smaller campaigns: the bell that is broken and then absent, Gowing's blackened stick, the blanc-mange, the stylographic pen, the cistern.
Argue that blaming the equipment lets Pooter keep his dignity, and that the pattern is also an exact record of a house run on a narrow income.
Close on the freehold: the one object in the book that is given rather than fought with.

discussionQuestions: Pooter writes down the jokes that failed as carefully as the ones that worked. Why would a man do that, and what would the book lose if he did not?
Carrie laughs at the dry rot joke and at Gowing's joke about the odd sock. Is she a better audience than the reader, or simply a kinder one?
The diary is torn up to light a fire, and Lupin values it by the pound. What is the book saying about its own worth?
Is Gowing a friend? Does the book expect us to think friendship requires liking?
Hardfur Huttle says respectability means dullness, and nobody at the table answers him. Does the book answer him?
Perkupp buys the Pooters their house. Is that a happy ending, or the sharpest thing in the book?

related.why: Published by the same Bristol firm three years earlier, another comic first person who files his own defeats without noticing; and its comic song was created on stage by one of the authors of the diary.

For Wemmick and the little castle at Walworth: a London clerk who makes a fortified private world out of a small suburban house, thirty years before Pooter did the same with a tin-tack and a Venetian blind.
Written three years after the book, and treating respectability as pure performance rather than an achievement to be defended; Wilde's people lie brilliantly where Pooter cannot lie at all.
The same London of clerks, lodgings, omnibuses and small suburban villas, written for a neighbouring magazine readership in the same years, and found sinister rather than comfortable.
The clerk seen from the employer's side of the counting-house, and a useful measure of Mr. Perkupp, who ends by buying his faithful servant a house without ever needing to be converted.
